title: SihtiSort: changing spike waveforms, stable source identities, and refutable merges
summary: SihtiSort turns the question of recognizing one changing sender into a synthetic spike-sorting benchmark. Clusters that alternate in time and share a spatial footprint may be assigned one neuron address with multiple waveform states. The preregistered crowded-recording gate failed; post-hoc sparse controls exposed a useful temporal-merge signal, while a later commit/refute/revise pull request failed to revise mistaken merges. This is source identification, not a proof of stable neural memory, cognitive character, or an online exploratory observer.

nodes.claim: Tests whether one physical neuron's identity can be retained when its extracellular spike waveform changes abruptly, using temporal cluster alternation, spatial footprint, refractory constraints, matching-pursuit residue subtraction, and a hypothesis ledger.
nodes.survived: After correcting the evaluator to one-to-one spike matching, the frozen five-recording test still recovered 7/20 mood neurons versus 6/20 for snapshot plus standard merge; the main +25-point gate failed. In the explicitly post-hoc spatially separated recordings, temporal merging recovered 20/20 versus 14/20, with 10/10 strong-mood neurons versus 4/10. Corrected overlap recall on the original test was 0.78 versus 0.25 for the no-sieve control, but matching pursuit is established prior art.
nodes.killed: The preregistered G0/G1 gates failed; the explicit five-second state prior added almost nothing, and the main results are synthetic, not real spike-sorting evidence. In follow-on PR #3 the firing-rate refuter never revised a merge, missed the two large-rate-gap pairs before a testable two-state hypothesis existed, and wrongly marked five of 34 'survived' merges; sub-channel position discrimination was post hoc. Distinct neurons taking turns can be observationally equivalent to one switching neuron when the available signals lack a separating cue.

edges.why: SihtiSort explicitly borrows the sieve/residue and re-examination vocabulary, but its residual is ordinary waveform-template matching pursuit rather than Sihti's image-operator residue decomposition. This is a conceptual echo, not a code fork or evidence that the same mechanism operates.

motifs.title: Keeping an address while appearances move is not the same as preserving meaning or behavior
motifs.description: SihtiSort tests continued physical source identity across different waveform states; MovingProblem tracks grounded semantic orientation under drifting representations; MovingTarget2 asks which query responses survive hidden phase motion. Their methods differ. SihtiSort's failed refuter makes a further boundary visible: temporal continuity can support a plausible address without making that identity identifiable, and untested alternatives may be lost in an upstream clustering stage.
